I would like to start off by saying that as someone who really loved Do the Right Thing I was very excited to watch this movie. I mean, who wouldn't after reading that premise right? The sheer concept of a black cop infiltrating the KKK immediately got my attention...yet this film almost completely falls apart on every level. The first and last 5 minutes are great. The last scene with Ron and Patrice especially actually had me lock tf in, that was a powerful way to wrap the story up in a way I never expected. Everything else is kinda ass. I just wanna say that the editing in this movie is unironically one of the worst I've seen. The shots have absolutely no continuity after cutting, it keeps cutting in the most awkward moments, the genuinely powerful speech at the beginning has some really goofy closeups of the audience for some reason, there's just endless examples of atrocious editing that made it impossible for me to have fun with the film. This movie should have been a comedy, but for some reason it's a terrible one even with a premise this silly. There's nothing snappy about the intentionally comedic lines, it's just kind of awkwardly lumbering in its own rhythm and it's not funny. The acting is fine but nothing memorable. Adam Driver gave a better performance in Megalopolis of all things than this movie. The social commentary here also is just surface level as hell and cheap. It's genuinely shocking coming from the man behind one of the most nuanced movies on race tensions, that the main thing explored here is white people are racist. Any room for nuance set up by the plot of the movie: Adam Driver wrestling with his Jew heritage, Patrice's, and her people in general, hatred of cops, Ron's weird insistence on believing in changing the system from inside never truly being explored nor challenged, the racist cop(s) in Ron's department, and so much more are just...dropped? They don't reach anywhere close to resolution nor is there any development with these themes, they're just mentioned briefly and discarded. Why does Ron need to be on the phone? Why can't Adam Driver just be on the phone and meeting them in person? The premise itself has holes, and throughout the entire movie I honestly don't know what our characters are doing in the KKK. Do they really learn anything of value? Do I, the audience, even learn anything from watching this movie? There's not even like a comical examination of KKK's weird activities and procedures like I thought they would, it's like there's barely any research done into the organisation you're making a movie about. The whole movie is just Adam Driver and Ron dicking around in the KKK and hearing white people spam hate speech. It's not entertaining, funny, nor educational. It's cheap . The fucking 5 minutes KKK cutscene in Django Unchained with Quentin Tarantino as a racist Klan member was like a thousand times more entertaining than this movie in a fraction of its screentime.

I left the film feeling very conflicted. Undoubtedly, the film is well-made, funny, and masterfully crafted. I found the writing to be hilarious and the comedic beats really hit well. The ending was pretty good, felt it could've been worked in better but still good. Here is my issue. It was copaganda. YES, I am aware that the film shows the "bad" police too and I am aware that it shows "different" perspectives. Though, to pretend like we are meant to root for anyone else but our protagonist Black police officer who will "change the system from the inside" is ridiculous. They even spelled out this topic clear as day, they had a literal argument about this. That was disgustingly neoliberalistic, it is to pretend MLK would even exist in the same way as he does without Malcolm X (El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz). After finding out Lee's company was paid over 200k to help "better" relationships between NYPD and the Black community, things started to get fishy. Boots Riley hit it on the nose, calling out that Stallworth, in real life, worked with COINTELPRO against Black radical organizations. The same organizations facing political assassinations by the United States government, relentlessly. The movie glazes over systemic issues of justice, portraying a false ideal of a utopian system that can really be changed without pressure from the outside. A single Black cop stops racism within a police department. How picturesque. We are told, indirectly, that Black activists in this movie are "too radical" and a danger. The comparison even clearly made between their actions and the KKK's. Disgusting horseshoe theory bullshit. I like Spike Lee, I like a lot of the work he has done. I actually enjoyed the simple aspect of viewing this movie. But my reviews have never been just about the quality of movie but also the message. This movie is not the message I want to see. Especially for one so bold in its message that it deliberately makes modern day connections for the audience. What should our takeaway be according to this film? Encourage oppressed people to take part in the system that is oppressing them, cause they can change it from the inside. Maybe I, as a Palestinian, should get involved in the Israeli Knesset. It's always a bit difficult to rate films based on true stories. It raises questions such as : should you aestheticize things that weren't ? Should a film's faithfulness to real events affect its rating ? Does it still need to be entertaining in the way it's directed ? In terms of pure feeling and a basic judgment, I can't help feeling that the film is wasted potential. It's only near the end that it comes close to the level of stress and tension that could have been present throughout the entire film, and it was only when real footage was shown for a few minutes that I felt genuinely hurt and outraged. Going back to the questions I raised at the beginning, I think the film tried too hard to stay entertaining and visually appealing, to the point of becoming almost comical by adding subtle humor to every scene and turning every character into a caricature. Or maybe white supremacists really were that ridiculous back then and I'm the one who's wrong ? But I think it's more likely a huge mistake on Spike Lee's part, combined with mid acting and mid direction. There's a serious lack of raw scenes showing the emotional struggles some of these characters may have gone through. The film almost gives the impression that social segregation wasn't all that violent, that racists were only a minority and that infiltrating a group of dangerous unstable sick individuals is just routine. And after a few quick searches, it becomes clear that the film is far from Ron Stallworth's real story. He first spent three years infiltrating black activists and radical black groups before infiltrating the KKK for nine months, not just one for a night and the other for a month. In conclusion, Spike Lee reduced reality to the story of a somewhat cool black cop infiltrating a group of somewhat stupid racists who do some not so nice things. But on the whole, it’s not a complete disaster with no substance or form. It’s just that looking at the film’s overall rating I get the impression that everyone has kind of agreed it’s a very good movie that represents the cause well. I suppose the intention was there, and the goal was still to highlight an important and underrepresented period of history, so let’s not be too harsh either.

Spike Lee remains one of cinema’s most essential voices. He gave us Malcolm X, a monumental achievement and a fearless tribute to El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz that never once feels interested in sanding down its rough edges or making itself easier to digest. But returning to BlacKkKlansman for a second viewing, that first watch exhilaration quickly wears off. What’s left is a film that gradually loses its footing, drifting away from the fierce, uncompromising anti-racist voice that has always defined Lee at his best. Instead of staying locked onto the realities of Black life in post civil rights America and the institutions working against it, the film settles for something noticeably safer. Its decision to weave in a broad, underdeveloped subplot about anti-Semitism only diffuses the film’s central force. Even more frustratingly, much of that thread revolves around a heavily fictionalized arc centered on Adam Driver’s character, one that has little basis in the memoir the film is based on. Rather than sharpening its argument, it broadens it into a universal lesson about hatred, smoothing away the specificity and righteous anger that have always defined Spike Lee’s cinema. In trying to speak to everyone, particularly a broader liberal audience, the film ends up muting the confrontational edge that makes Lee’s best work so singular. It feels less like a filmmaker challenging his audience and more like one reassuring it, trading uncompromising political fury for polished Hollywood respectability.

Assistir a Infiltrado na Klan em 2026, 8 anos após sua estreia nas salas de cinema, é olhar por um monóculo fotográfico de lente embaçada. Em menos de uma década, o zeitgest já se metamorfoseara de tal maneira que o filme de Spike Lee é, no frigir dos ovos, indesvencilhável do clima  da política ocidental de 2018 - seja para o bem ou para o mal. É facilmente perceptível ao se analisar a recepção do longa-metragem que, sobre as condições de seu primeiro lançamento, foi possível que a empreitada dos "irmãos Stallworth" reproduzida em tela potencializasse uma apoteótica comoção ideológica sobre sua audiência. O  notável valor motivacional das cenas da KKK e do Movimento Negro - as quais o idealizador justapõe mais de uma vez, consciente e ironicamente, pela montagem paralela tão querida por D. W. Graffith - são capazes de afetar ao espectador graças ao desconforto ou a empatia. Porém, não creio ser possível dizer o mesmo sobre o aparato textual e formal de sua obra. Indeciso entre representar sua aventura policial como um retrato cosmético capaz de desfrutar assumidamente do apelo psicológico de seu aspecto retro , com suas superfícies polidas e lustradas; uma homenagem direta às sensibilidades nutridas pelo cinema setentista, do split screen ao grão do filme; ou um comentário anacrônico, cru e comovente sobre a violência racial, Lee não finca-pé sobre nenhuma das oportunidades estéticas que tais possibilidades o permitem, cruzando tais iniciativas em um híbrido no mínimo mal aproveitado. Lapsos de genialidade na direção ou inventividade na montagem não conseguem ocultar uma obra fundamentada no maniqueísmo entre forças opostas - cartunizadas ao máximo na pura bondade ou maldade, arquetipizadas na estudante radicalizada de rostinho bonito e no klansman retardado bobão - que só conseguem funcionar como cosmos narrativo quando mediadas e superadas pelo ímpeto individual do good cop boa pinta. Ao mesmo tempo, questões que fujam da obviedade identitária (como a ambiguidade entre a branquitude e a etnia judaica pautada no personagem de Driver e toda a problemática do racismo como opressão sistemática e estrutural da nação branca estadunidense) são propriamente escanteadas em favor de um thriller policial que deixa a desejar, com excessão de uma ou outra sequência dinâmica na segunda metade da minutagem. Assim, Spike Lee busca filmar suas personagens diante da necessidade de atuação civil e corporativa sem, por outro lado, permitir-se explorar devidamente as ambiguidades técnicas e ideológicas de seu projeto artístico. BlacKkKlansman , sobretudo, é um filme pouco catártico e corajoso estetica e textualmente para o papel de cinema político que buscou exercer.

BlacKkKlansman está cargadísima de problemáticas sociales y raciales, o sea, ésta directamente gira en torno a una historia real sobre la secta racista más conocida de la historia. Y claramente banco el mensaje, la crítica y lo absurdo que resulta todo esto. El tema es que la película nunca me llevó un punto más allá. La premisa es cuanto menos entretenida de ver, y tiene situaciones que en el papel deberían ser tensísimas o incómodas, pero en ningún momento percibí que la película llegara a explotar realmente. Todo avanzaba y rara vez sentía que algo tuviera verdadero peso, incluso la historia termina siendo bastante predecible. Y aunque no tengo ningún problema con los finales felices, este me pareció demasiado hollywoodense para tratarse de una historia basada en hechos reales. De hecho, el cierre terminó de confirmarme esa sensación, ya que en vez de sentir que la película había llegado naturalmente a un punto de quiebre, sentí que Spike necesitaba detenerse para recordarme cuál era el mensaje que acababa de ver durante dos horas. Tal vez también tengan algo que ver las expectativas. Ya que ésta, junto a Malcolm X y Do the Right Thing son películas que llevaba muchísimo tiempo queriendo ver, y entre las críticas y todo lo que se escucha sobre ellas, terminé llegando con las expectativas por las nubes. Esperaba que esto me demostrara por qué Spike Lee ES Spike Lee, pero no pasó. Aún con todo esto, le tengo una fe increíble a las otras dos.

We are meant to sympathize with the struggles of our main character when his girlfriend challenges him and is very upset when she finds out that he's a cop, because she just 'doesn't understand'. We are meant to see Ron's girlfriend, Patrice, as some radical who just can't see past her pig hating lenses and trust her well meaning cop boyfriend, who only wants the best for their people. One of the biggest critiques people have of America's justice system, racism aside, is that it doesn't rehabilitate — it punishes. This seems ideal when you consider that pedophiles and other offenders of violent crimes will suffer, but it doesn't account for the fact that people like thieves and loiterers are also in there suffering. Some people think it's adequate, but it doesn't actually do anything proactive to prevent crime and often causes more issues than solutions. This is often something socialists and pro black activists complain about, and during the Black Panther era, dismantling the prison system was very, very important to their politics. It's almost like the writers wanted to paint the police as heroes and convince those watching that movements like the pro-Black movements need police officers to keep them safe. The movie is meant to make us feel like you can fix the system from the inside, and it humanized police officers and the system in a way that made them feel more like victims than perpetrators. The real life story is certainly compelling but the story decides to fictionalize some incredibly important aspects such as Flip’s identity, Ron’s personal philosophy, and Patrice. Four stars for a movie that spends two hours as a funny, stylish period piece and then, in the last three minutes, cuts to Charlottesville footage and turns the whole thing into an indictment of the audience for relaxing. Spike Lee's structural argument is the thing that makes "BlacKkKlansman" more than a caper: the Klan of 1972 talks about immigration, crime, and America First in language you can hear on television tonight, and Ron Stallworth's white partner has to physically embody the whiteness Ron performs on the phone. The voice is the whole movie. Code-switching as literal undercover work, and Adam Driver's Flip discovering that his own Jewishness, which he'd never thought about, was always at stake. "The Birth of a Nation" sequence intercut with Harry Belafonte describing a lynching is the best-edited scene of the year: cinema as recruitment tool and cinema as testimony, on the same screen. What keeps it at four: the police procedural stuff soft-pedals the institution in ways Lee's own filmography usually wouldn't, and Boots Riley's public criticism about the cop framing has real merit. But that ending. Four stars. All power to all the people, and put the whole thing on the record.

I rewatched BlacKkKlansman today. Stop me if you’ve heard this before: There’s no such thing as *just* a bad apple, and “good” cops are automatically implicated by the very system they participate in. Even the black cops, the liberal cops, and especially the “my uncle” cops uphold white supremacy by joining a chapter in its legacy, treating their other brothers in blue like family, letting minorities be squashed and slaughtered under the knee like bugs. You’ve probably heard this rhetoric/explanation before and chances are, you agree with it because the issue of cops killing black people never stops, and your profile keeps growing, and maybe you’ve been a victim of police abuse. Or maybe you don’t, and maybe you think there are good cops, and maybe you think that those who say this are simply shaping their perspective on a few negative experiences… but also, maybe you just don’t know. Maybe you believe in one side or the other, but you have no experience in the matter. Maybe you just haven’t seen this rhetoric’s assertions put to practice, and maybe that neutrality is what you are. I want to clear the air and say I do agree with the idea that one rotten apple spoils the bunch, but it’s something that’s often interrogated from the perspective of the victim- or in more racist conditions, the perspective of the cop. But rarely is the depiction of this allowed to unfold. It’s either assumed as fact or assumed as false, and by taking these roads people refuse to engage with it and it simply becomes doctrine. Whether you think that’s good or bad is up to you and what you value in your mind more, but if I had to characterize exactly what BlacKkKlansman is about, it would be this war and the real conditions that allowed this rhetoric to become either doctrine or slander to so many. Lee may have said otherwise, but his movie often speaks for itself- it is unafraid to depict the countless hypocrisies that plague Ron Stallworth and his buddies in their operation (or crusade) to end the Ku Klux Klan. And despite that, you’re never quite brought against Ron for his cop ties. He’s often forced to participate in hypocrisies by the very nature of an oppressive, ingrained social and political system- even if he shows spunk, he still has to spy on Kwame Ture and defend David Duke. “It’s not his fault” isn’t the point- the point is that he’s made to do this, and the good he does ends up being forgotten or reversed or faded over time. You can’t help but sympathize with his struggle as he desperately wants to serve black liberation, but you also can’t help but totally agree with Patrice by the end- she can’t sleep with the enemy. That ending is just the final punctuation to this. What the hell can Ron Stallworth do against times like this? The fight goes on, but cops are nowhere to be found… well, nowhere to be found on the correct side. It’s hopeless, painful, and bloody from his perspective- and that’s the whole point. The rhetoric that all cops are bad isn’t told from hatred or petty grievances- it’s told from a moment of haunting like this, which you can actually connect with. While I don’t think anything can ever top Do the Right Thing, I’m always seated for whatever this director puts out. I think what made that film an all timer for me is it asks a lot of questions about what is the “Right Thing”, particularly when it comes to inequality. I think this movie kind of builds on that theme, but amplifies it to a much higher degree with greater consequences. A fitting thing for when this movie came out that is still the same today. Politics are much more polarizing today. But, I also think Lee is much more unapologetic to excuses for racism than even his early films. The last 5 minutes of this lays it out clear. There are still limits to changing the system from within and hate has been on the rise again. Movie MVP: Going to go with Spike here. The director adds such a cool groove to this film that makes it feel both like a film in the 1970s, when it takes place, and in the late 2010s. It is bleak subject matter for sure, especially when the director uses real world examples of racial injustice and racism. There’s an interesting question in here of “well, why aren’t you doing more?” when fighting injustice that affects everyone.
